text: v01: “Scattered abroad” renders the diaspora, the dispersion of Jewish communities. “The twelve tribes” preserves James's way of addressing his readers. “Servant” renders a word also used for an enslaved person.

v12–15: The Greek word-family can mean trial, testing, or temptation. Verse 12 concerns enduring a trial; verses 13–15 concern enticement to evil. The pinned Greek in v12 leaves the one who promised unstated; “God” identifies the understood referent.

v01–03: The compact wording in v01 links faith in Jesus Christ with glory; Fluent retains “our glorious Lord Jesus Christ.” “Gathering” in v02 translates synagōgē, also the source of the English word “synagogue.” Verse 3 follows the pinned Greek's “stand, or sit there below my footstool”; other witnesses place “there” with “stand” and read “sit here.”

v01–03: The compact wording in v01 links faith in Jesus Christ with glory; Fluent retains “our glorious Lord Jesus Christ.” “Gathering” in v02 translates synagōgē, also the source of the English word “synagogue.” Verse 3 follows the pinned Greek's “stand, or sit there below my footstool”; other witnesses place “there” with “stand” and read “sit here.”

v07–08: The honorable name is described as having been spoken over the readers. Verse 8 quotes Leviticus 19:18. “Royal law” preserves the text's royal language without deciding its full significance for the reader.
v20: The pinned SBLGNT text reads “useless” or “inactive.” Some witnesses read “dead,” the word used in vv17 and 26.

v01–03: The word rendered “pleasures” differs from the word for “desire” in 1:14. Verse 2 is difficult to punctuate. Fluent retains the sequence “You want … You murder and covet … You quarrel” without adding a causal “so” before “murder.”

v03: The Greek describes gold and silver as corroded. The words “like fire” can attach to the eating of flesh or to the following sentence about storing treasure. Fluent retains the former reading; the pinned SBLGNT edition punctuates with the latter attachment.

v03: The Greek describes gold and silver as corroded. The words “like fire” can attach to the eating of flesh or to the following sentence about storing treasure. Fluent retains the former reading; the pinned SBLGNT edition punctuates with the latter attachment.

v04–06: “Lord of hosts” renders the divine title Kyrios Sabaōth; hosts are armies or multitudes. Verse 5 has “on a day of slaughter”; Fluent retains “hearts” and the slaughter image. The final clause of v06 may be read as a statement or a question. Fluent retains “does not resist you”; SBLGNT punctuates it as a question, “Does he not resist you?”

v07–11: The early and late rains belong to the agricultural cycle. The Lord's coming and the judge at the door retain the passage's urgency. “The outcome the Lord brought about” in v11 can also be understood as the Lord's purpose or intended end.

v19–20: The Greek of v20 refers to saving “his life/soul,” but the possessive's referent is disputed. “A life” leaves that question open. “Cover many sins” retains the covering image rather than explaining how it happens.

v04: ἀφυστερέω (aphystereō)
Withhold or deprive; the verb read by the pinned SBLGNT text here.

v01–02: The opening can also be understood as “When God began to create …” leading into the following scene. This draft retains the independent opening sentence. “The deep” names the waters already present in the scene; the wording does not itself explain their origin.

v01–02: The opening can also be understood as “When God began to create …” leading into the following scene. This draft retains the independent opening sentence. “The deep” names the waters already present in the scene; the wording does not itself explain their origin.

v26–28: The speaker says “us” and “our” without identifying the plural referents. “Humanity” renders the collective adam. Verse 27 moves from a singular human referent to “them”; the English uses “them” for the collective while keeping male and female explicit. “Rule” and “subdue” retain the force of the source verbs.

v02–04: The pinned Hebrew says God completed the work on the seventh day. “Rested” also means ceased. Verse 4 begins an account formula repeated throughout Genesis. Its second sentence introduces the garden narrative with “earth and heaven,” reversing the order of the opening phrase.

v17–18: “When you eat” is literally “in the day of your eating”; “certainly die” preserves the emphatic construction. “A helper who corresponds to him” renders ezer kenegdo. The expression names help and correspondence; it does not itself call the helper inferior.

v15: “Offspring” translates zera, also the word for seed. The Hebrew refers back to the woman's offspring with a masculine singular pronoun; the noun can have a collective sense. This draft retains offspring and uses “their” without identifying a particular later figure. The same verb is used for the blows to head and heel.

v15: “Offspring” translates zera, also the word for seed. The Hebrew refers back to the woman's offspring with a masculine singular pronoun; the noun can have a collective sense. This draft retains offspring and uses “their” without identifying a particular later figure. The same verb is used for the blows to head and heel.

v20–24: Eve's name is linked in the narrative with living. God's speech in v22 breaks off before a completed main clause; the dash preserves that interruption. Cherubim are named guardians; the text gives no physical description of them here.

v01: “Had sexual relations” renders the Hebrew idiom “knew.” Cain's name is linked with Eve's verb qaniti, “I have acquired/produced.” Her phrase involving the LORD is compact and disputed; this draft retains the reading “with the LORD's help.”

v01: “Had sexual relations” renders the Hebrew idiom “knew.” Cain's name is linked with Eve's verb qaniti, “I have acquired/produced.” Her phrase involving the LORD is compact and disputed; this draft retains the reading “with the LORD's help.”
v08: The pinned Hebrew says Cain spoke to Abel but does not give the words he spoke. No invitation to the field has been supplied in the main text.

v01–05: Adam can name a person or humanity. The image and likeness language recalls 1:26–27. The ages follow the pinned Hebrew and are not converted into a modern chronology or explained as another unit of time.

v01–04: The passage does not identify the “sons of God” or explain the Nephilim. “Beautiful” follows the source's description of the daughters. The wording “any they chose” retains the taking and choice without adding an account of the women's consent.

v20–22: The offering consists of burnt offerings from clean animals and birds. The LORD's smelling and inner speech remain in the translation. “Even though” in v21 interprets the connective ki; “because” is another possible reading. The promise preserves all four pairs of earth's rhythms.

v09–17: The covenant explicitly includes descendants and nonhuman creatures. “Bow” is the ordinary Hebrew word for a bow, including a weapon; its appearance in the clouds is a rainbow. The translation preserves the word without requiring a single interpretation of that resonance.

v01–07: This genealogy presents peoples and territories through family lines. It is not a map of modern countries or a classification of modern races. Mizraim is the Hebrew name associated with Egypt; it is retained as an ancestral name here. Dodanim in v04 follows the pinned Hebrew.

v21–25: Verse 21 can identify either Shem or Japheth as the older brother; this draft retains Shem as older. “Peleg” echoes the verb for dividing, but the verse does not explain what kind of division occurred.

v21–25: Verse 21 can identify either Shem or Japheth as the older brother; this draft retains Shem as older. “Peleg” echoes the verb for dividing, but the verse does not explain what kind of division occurred.

v10–26: The family line keeps the ages of the pinned Hebrew text, including Eber's 430 years after Peleg's birth. The age followed by three sons in v26 does not establish simultaneous births or necessarily their birth order.

v14–18: The land promise follows Lot’s departure. The descendants-as-dust comparison concerns their number. “Forever” retains the enduring force of the promise without adding a modern political identification.

v09–12: The three mammals are described with a term conventionally read as three years old. The birds are not divided. Deep sleep and fearful darkness are retained without adding an explanation of Abram’s inner state.
v13–16: Four hundred years and the fourth generation are both preserved. The first duration’s relation to residence, enslavement, and oppression is not resolved by a supplied chronology.

v01–06: Hagar is both Egyptian and enslaved. Sarai gives her as a wife while remaining her mistress. The account preserves these unequal relationships and does not supply Hagar’s consent. “Build a family” in v02 retains the Hebrew building image.

v01–10: The account moves among the LORD, three men, plural address, and a singular speaker. The translation preserves those shifts. “My Lord” in v03 follows the Hebrew pointing; a respectful address to a visitor is another reading.

v30–38: The older daughter’s claim that no man is available is her speech, not a narrator’s statement that every other man has died. The account of incest preserves Lot’s stated unawareness and the daughters’ stated aim of descendants. Moab and Ben-ammi introduce people groups, not a modern racial classification.

v11–13: The absence of fear of God is Abraham’s assumption. His explanation of Sarah’s kinship remains his speech. In v13 Elohim is accompanied by a plural verb; the draft retains the customary God reading without erasing the grammatical difficulty from review.

v11–13: The absence of fear of God is Abraham’s assumption. His explanation of Sarah’s kinship remains his speech. In v13 Elohim is accompanied by a plural verb; the draft retains the customary God reading without erasing the grammatical difficulty from review.

v12–18: Ishmael’s twelve leaders recall 17:20. The final clause in v18 is difficult: its verb usually means fall, and it has been read as settlement or death. This draft uses settlement with a collective referent and retains facing, recalling 16:12; hostility is another understanding of the phrase.
v34: The names of Esau’s wives and their fathers differ in 36:2–3. This translation preserves each passage’s names rather than silently making them agree.

v01–13: The chapter preserves Rachel and Leah’s anguish, rivalry, and claims about the births. Bilhah and Zilpah bear four sons while enslaved; the text does not record their consent to the arrangements.

v40: The wording about facing the flock toward marked animals is difficult. The translation retains the visual arrangement and separation of Jacob’s herds without supplying a complete breeding theory.
v55: English Genesis 31:55 corresponds to Hebrew Genesis 32:1. The verse is bound to that full source record, including its versification note.
v01–32: English Genesis 32:1–32 corresponds to Hebrew Genesis 32:2–33 in the pinned source. Hebrew Genesis 32:1 appears as English 31:55. Every public verse here is bound to its exact Hebrew record.
v04–05: Jacob calls himself Esau’s servant and Esau his lord. ‘Resident foreigner’ retains his sojourner status with Laban; the servants he lists among his property are enslaved people.
v11: ‘Mothers along with their children’ preserves a concrete Hebrew expression for indiscriminate destruction.
v09, 11: Esau says he has ‘plenty’; Jacob says he has ‘everything.’ The wording preserves the contrast without making either claim a financial inventory.

v15–19: Chief translates alluf, a title for a clan or tribal leader. Korah appears among Oholibamah’s sons in verse 14 and among the chiefs descended from Eliphaz in verse 16; the lists are not harmonized.
v31: The narrator locates Edom’s kings before a king ruled over the Israelites. The translation preserves the statement without supplying a date or theory of composition.

v39: The pinned Hebrew reads Hadar; Hadad appears in some related textual traditions. Mehetabel’s mother and maternal grandfather are named, an unusual preservation of a woman’s lineage in the king list.

v16: The Hebrew says that God will answer Pharaoh with shalom—peace, well-being, or wholeness. The answer includes both abundance and severe famine, so “answer of peace” preserves the striking expression.
v47: “By the handfuls” preserves an unusual Hebrew expression for the land’s abundant yield.
v07: The brothers report questions about their family that are not included in the earlier narrated exchange. The translation preserves the difference between the scenes.
v34: The final verb can mean to become drunk. The translation retains its force rather than reducing the meal’s ending to general happiness.
v04–08: Joseph names his brothers’ sale of him, then repeatedly speaks of God sending him ahead to preserve life. Both descriptions remain part of his address to the brothers.
v07: Great deliverance can also be understood as a great body of survivors. “Remnant” retains a term used elsewhere in Scripture for a surviving community.
v15–16: The blessing places ‘God’ and ‘the angel’ in parallel descriptions. It does not explain their relationship here. The translation retains that compressed form.

v5: The Hebrew gives seventy, as in Genesis 46:27. The ancient Greek gives seventy-five. Exodus speaks here of Jacob’s descendants; the earlier household count should not silently replace its wording.
v22: ‘Ask’ does not itself mean ‘borrow.’ ‘Plunder’ retains the force of the closing image; the verse does not promise that the requested goods will be returned.
v10–12: Moses describes a heavy or slow mouth and tongue. The passage does not identify a particular speech disorder. God’s response retains its difficult claim about speech, hearing, and sight.

v3: The Hebrew states that God was not known to the ancestors by the name YHWH, represented here by LORD. Genesis nevertheless uses this name in their stories and speech (for example, Genesis 15:2). The translation preserves the statement without inserting ‘fully’ or turning it into a question.
v2: ‘Made a mockery of’ can also mean ‘dealt harshly with.’ The verb retains a force stronger than simply ‘did things in Egypt.’
v25–26: Moses demands provision for sacrifices and insists that all their livestock go too. ‘Not a hoof’ preserves the concrete image of leaving no animal behind.
v22: The word rendered ‘basin’ can also mean ‘threshold.’ The translation retains the basin reading; it does not add a separate rite at the threshold.
v11–12: ‘Among the gods’ and ‘the earth swallowed them’ retain the poem’s own comparisons and images. They are not replaced with explanations drawn from later doctrinal debates.
v34–35: The testimony and the forty years look ahead beyond the present camp. The translation preserves those forward-looking references rather than moving them to a later point in the story.

v14: Memorial — zikkaron
Something that preserves remembrance, here a written record.

v5–6: The promise joins covenant obedience, Israel’s place among the peoples, and God’s ownership of the whole earth. ‘Kingdom of priests’ preserves the compact Hebrew expression rather than specifying a later political or religious structure.

v3–6: ‘Before me’ can express presence or opposition; it does not merely rank one god above others. The following commands forbid making images, bowing to them, and serving them. The warning about fathers and children retains both the generational consequences and ‘those who hate me.’

v10, 17: The lists retain male and female slaves as part of the ancient household. Rest extends to them, livestock, and resident foreigners. Their inclusion in the coveting prohibition reflects the social conditions of the text.

v5: Jealous — qanna’
Demanding exclusive loyalty; the word retains the force of the image rather than reducing it to preference.

v2–11: These rulings distinguish a purchased Hebrew man, a wife he already had, a wife supplied by his master, and a daughter sold by her father. The release terms differ; the translation preserves these distinctions and the ownership language.

v8: The written Hebrew has “who did not designate her”; the traditional reading has “who designated her for himself.” The translation follows the reading while preserving both forms in the source record.

v20–21: “Avenged” leaves the penalty unspecified here. Verse 21 makes survival for a day or two decisive without explicitly describing the slave’s later condition. “His money” preserves the Hebrew’s stark description of the enslaved person as the owner’s property.

v22–25: “Her children come out” does not explicitly say whether the birth results in death or survival. The following “harm” is also not assigned explicitly to the woman or her children. Miscarriage and premature delivery are disputed readings. The paired injuries retain the passage’s formal pattern. [Translator discussion](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Exodus+21&version=NET).
v2–3: “Breaking in” refers to a break-in or tunneling entry. The law distinguishes this case from one in which the sun has risen; the translation retains that stated distinction.

v20–21, 28: The angel is not named. “My name is within him” retains the source’s expression of divine authority. “The hornet” may describe insects or function as an image for what drives the peoples out; the translation preserves the image. [Translator discussion](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Exodus+23&version=NET).

v31: “Sea of Reeds” is the Hebrew name also used in 13:18 and 15:4. The sea of the Philistines is the Mediterranean. “The River” is commonly understood as the Euphrates. The text preserves these ancient geographic designations.

v10–11: The account says both that the leaders saw God and that he did not lay his hand on them. The translation leaves these statements together without adding an explanation of the vision. “Sapphire” represents the ancient blue-stone term sappir; modern mineral identification is uncertain.

v17: The atonement cover is traditionally called the “mercy seat.” Here it is the gold cover over the ark; the translation retains its association with atonement without describing it as a chair. [Translator discussion](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Exodus+25&version=NET).

v33–35: The lampstand has six side branches and a central shaft. The ornament descriptions are compact: the translation retains the repeated three-cup pattern, four cups on the lampstand itself, and a bud beneath each pair of branches.

v30: The Urim and Thummim are associated with seeking divine decisions. Their form and the procedure for using them are not described here. “Judgment” retains the connection with the breastpiece’s name in verse 15; it need not mean condemnation.

v17: “Caught his breath” preserves the bodily image of the Hebrew verb, also used for the refreshment of workers and animals in 23:12. Here the image is applied to God after creation. [Translator discussion](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Exodus+31&version=NET).
v18: “Finger of God” retains the ancient image of divine action; compare the same expression in 8:19. The verse identifies the tablets as stone without explaining the writing process.

v11, 20–23: “Face to face” describes speech compared with a conversation between friends. Later, seeing God’s face is forbidden. The passage retains both expressions, along with the images of God’s hand and back.
v14: The grain descriptions may describe a single preparation or different forms of early grain. The draft keeps the descriptions together without adding a precise recipe.

v20–22: The Hebrew names Aaron and his sons but then says “he is anointed.” Verse 22 speaks of an anointed successor. The draft preserves both the anointing occasion and the description of a regular offering.

v09–10: Prepared grain offerings are assigned to the officiating priest; the next verse assigns offerings mixed with oil or dry to all Aaron’s sons equally. The draft preserves both rules without inserting an explanation of their relationship.

v30–34: “Wave offering” retains the term used in Exodus 29. The exact ritual movement is uncertain. The breast belongs to Aaron and his sons; the right thigh goes to the son who handles this sacrifice’s blood and fat.
v31: The pinned Hebrew reads “I commanded.” Some ancient versions read “I was commanded,” as in verse 35.
v07: The Hebrew includes the people in both atonement clauses. The ancient Greek version instead has “your household” in the first clause; the draft follows the pinned Hebrew.

v13–19: Several identifications are uncertain. “Eagle” may designate a griffon vulture, and “ostrich” may designate an owl. Other raptor and owl names also remain provisional. “Flying creatures” preserves the category that includes the bat.
v10: “Make atonement over it” preserves the Hebrew wording. It can also be understood as making atonement for the goat or using it to make atonement.
v14: The opening Hebrew clause repeats “life” in a compressed construction. Both this clause and the following prohibition retain the close identification of blood and life.
v17–18: “Marry” renders “take,” used here with women as its objects. Verse 18 retains the sister relationship and the rivalry between wives, with the restriction “while your wife is alive.”
v10: The pinned Hebrew repeats the adultery clause. The repetition is preserved here.

v27–32: “Deny yourselves” retains the expression used in 16:29–31. It is associated with fasting, but the Hebrew does not simply use the verb “fast.” Verse 29 says “cut off”; verse 30 separately says that God will “destroy” the person. The evening of the ninth begins the observance of the tenth day.

v19–22: The text states matching bodily injury and then repeats the distinction between replacing an animal and the death penalty for killing a human. The translation retains those formulations rather than replacing them with a later interpretation of how restitution was administered. “One rule” concerns the foreigner and native-born within this legal setting.
v30: “Walled city” follows the Hebrew reading tradition, “which has a wall.” The written form is “not,” producing a different sense if taken on its own. Both forms are preserved in the source record.

v33: The opening Hebrew clause is difficult: literally, roughly, “and whoever redeems from the Levites.” The draft retains that direction of redemption. Other readings make a Levite the redeemer or understand acquisition from Levites. The following Jubilee release of the sold house is clearer. No “not” has been added to repair the sentence.

v33: The opening Hebrew clause is difficult: literally, roughly, “and whoever redeems from the Levites.” The draft retains that direction of redemption. Other readings make a Levite the redeemer or understand acquisition from Levites. The following Jubilee release of the sold house is clearer. No “not” has been added to repair the sentence.
v01: The “figured stone” is an uncertain kind of carved or decorated stone installation. The preposition can mean bowing down “on it” or “before it”; the translation retains the first possibility.

v02–08: The opening expression links a special vow with an assessed value for a person. The exact vow procedure is not explained. The listed amounts vary by age and sex; the translation retains them without making them statements about a person’s dignity or supplying a theory for the differences.
v14: Reuel is the name in the pinned Hebrew here; 1:14 has Deuel. Some textual witnesses read Deuel here as well. The draft preserves the difference in its source.
v14: Reuel is the name in the pinned Hebrew here; 1:14 has Deuel. Some textual witnesses read Deuel here as well. The draft preserves the difference in its source.
v03: The thirty-to-fifty service range is retained here. Numbers 8:24 gives a starting age of twenty-five; the translation does not silently make the passages agree.

v06: Taḥash is an uncertain skin or leather material, also named in Exodus 25–26. The text does not securely identify an animal species. “Put its carrying poles in place” preserves the instruction here; Exodus 25:15 says the ark’s poles are not to be removed. The precise action is not explained.
v24–27: Drinking is stated in verse 24 and taken up again after the offering in verses 26–27. The repeated instructions are retained without adding a required number of separate drinks.

v24–26: The blessing addresses Israel with singular “you.” It repeats the LORD’s name three times and preserves the images of a shining and lifted face. The language expresses gracious attention, ending with peace.
v12–83: Each tribe’s gifts are recounted in full, with the same quantities and categories. The repetition also preserves each leader’s name and place in the twelve-day sequence.

v35–36: The Hebrew text marks these two invocations with inverted nun signs before and after them. Their precise function is debated; both verses are retained in place. “Myriads of thousands” preserves the expansive expression in verse 36, whose compressed wording requires supplying the relation “to” in English.
v4: “Rabble” preserves the narrator’s disparaging term for a group among the people. The verse does not identify their ethnicity.

v8: The expression describing the manna’s taste is difficult. “Rich oil” retains its oil comparison; other renderings include fresh oil or cakes made with oil. Exodus 16:31 gives a different comparison, which is not substituted here.

v25–26: The pinned Hebrew says the elders did not prophesy again; some ancient interpretations understand the same consonants as saying they did not cease. Eldad and Medad are described as registered, but their relation to the count of seventy is not made explicit.

v3: “Humble” can also convey meekness or lowliness. An interpretation emphasizing affliction has been proposed. The written and read spellings are both preserved in the source record; this translation follows the adjective reading.

v32–33: The devouring land, enormous inhabitants and grasshopper comparison belong to the scouts’ report. The translation preserves their claims without turning them into independent measurements or explaining how they knew what the inhabitants thought.

v36–50: These public verse numbers correspond to Hebrew 17:1–15. Public chapter 17 begins with Hebrew 17:16. All source records, including the numbering annotations, remain preserved in the revision ledger.

v22: God of the spirits of all flesh
A title linking God with the life or spirits of living beings; compare Numbers 27:16. The phrase is not reduced to a later theory about bodies and souls.
v19: The covenant of salt is an image of an enduring bond. The verse preserves that image without explaining a particular salt ritual.
v21: The person sprinkling the water must wash clothes. The separate clause about touching the water explicitly adds uncleanness until evening; the draft preserves that distinction.
v24: The pinned Hebrew says the Ammonite boundary was strong. An alternative textual reading names Jazer; it is not substituted into the draft.
v20–22: Permission to go is followed by anger because Balaam goes. The account does not explicitly supply a motive that resolves this tension. The draft preserves both statements.

v19–20: The statement about God’s reliability answers the attempt to reverse the blessing. The translation preserves its claim without adding a general explanation of every biblical passage about God relenting.

v6–7: Aloes are aromatic trees in this image; the plant’s precise identity is uncertain. The seed-and-water language evokes both fertility and descendants. Agag is the name in the pinned Hebrew; this verse does not identify a particular later king.

v11–13: The repeated word for zeal can also mean jealousy. The account attributes the turning away of anger and the covenant of peace to the LORD; the translation keeps those claims alongside the killing, without adding a doctrinal explanation of it.

v1: This public verse combines two Hebrew records: the final line of Hebrew chapter 25, “After the plague,” and Hebrew 26:1. Both records, including their source annotations, are preserved separately in the revision ledger.

v9–11: The census pauses to recall Dathan, Abiram and Korah. It explicitly says Korah was swallowed and that his sons did not die. The draft preserves both statements rather than broadening the deaths to every descendant.

v5: Clan
A named family group. The repeated ancestor-and-clan pairs preserve the structure of the genealogical record.

v5: Ephah and hin
An ephah measures dry goods and a hin measures liquids. The ancient units preserve the stated ratios without falsely precise modern conversions.
v1–16: These public verses correspond to Hebrew 30:2–17. Each complete Hebrew record, including its numbering annotation, remains bound in the ledger.

v2–5: The chapter distinguishes a man’s obligation from that of a young woman in her father’s household. The father’s silence confirms her obligation; his objection is tied to the day he hears. The translation preserves those unequal roles and their stated limits.

v5, 8, 12: “Forgive” is the ordinary Hebrew forgiveness verb. Here it addresses the woman’s release from a vow that her father or husband has canceled; the draft retains both the legal context and the divine action.

v5, 8, 12: “Forgive” is the ordinary Hebrew forgiveness verb. Here it addresses the woman’s release from a vow that her father or husband has canceled; the draft retains both the legal context and the divine action.

v6–8: The holy articles carried by Phinehas are not identified. “Every male” describes the campaign here; verse 17 later commands the killing of captive boys. The draft preserves both statements without changing “male” to “soldier” or claiming the death of every Midianite everywhere.

v20–24: The repeated “before the LORD” gives the military pledge a divine as well as communal setting. “Free of your obligation” renders language of being clear or guiltless after fulfilling the pledge. “Your sin will find you out” retains the image of sin pursuing the wrongdoer.

v8, 11, 36: Verse 8 uses Hahiroth after Pi-hahiroth in verse 7. It names the wilderness of Etham, while Exodus 15:22 names Shur in its account. The draft preserves each passage’s wording. Sin and Zin are also distinct names in this itinerary.
v11: The Hebrew calls the eastern side of the Sea of Chinnereth its “shoulder.” “Ridge” preserves the elevated edge of the landscape rather than treating the word as a human body part.

v19–23: The intentional cases name hatred, hostility and deliberate action. “Deliberately” in verse 20 has the image of lying in wait behind it. The contrasting cases retain the absence of hostility, intent to harm and awareness of the other person.

v4: Cubit
An ancient length unit associated with the forearm. The original unit preserves the stated measurements without falsely precise modern conversions.

v11–12: The women marry their paternal cousins. Their names appear here in the order Mahlah, Tirzah, Hoglah, Milcah and Noah, differing from the order in Numbers 26–27. The draft preserves this order.

v2: Inheritance
The land assigned within Israel’s families and tribes. The daughters retain their inheritance while the marriage rule keeps it within the ancestral tribe.

v37–39: Moses says that the LORD was angry with him because of the people. The draft retains his statement; compare Numbers 20:12. The children's not knowing good from evil is stated without defining an age threshold.

v37–39: Moses says that the LORD was angry with him because of the people. The draft retains his statement; compare Numbers 20:12. The children's not knowing good from evil is stated without defining an age threshold.

v10–12, 20–23: These historical asides name earlier inhabitants and the peoples who replaced them. Verse 12 compares the process with Israel's possession of land; the translation preserves the retrospective wording.
v33: The Hebrew written form has “his son”; the traditional read form has “his sons.” The draft follows the read form. Both are preserved in the source record.

v37: After the plural “your fathers,” the Hebrew shifts to singular forms, “his descendants after him.” The draft takes these collectively with the fathers. A reference to a particular ancestor is also possible. “By his presence” preserves the wording without inserting a named intermediary.
v4–5: “Face to face” stands beside Moses' mediation and the earlier statement that the people saw no form. The translation retains all three descriptions.

v12–15: This account says “Observe” the Sabbath and grounds the command in Israel's enslavement and liberation. It explicitly gives male and female slaves rest like their masters. Exodus 20:8–11 says “Remember” and gives a creation rationale; the draft preserves each account's wording.

v4: The short Hebrew statement permits more than one arrangement: “the LORD our God, the LORD is one” or “the LORD is our God, the LORD alone.” The draft retains “one” and leaves this consequential alternative visible here.

v4: The short Hebrew statement permits more than one arrangement: “the LORD our God, the LORD is one” or “the LORD is our God, the LORD alone.” The draft retains “one” and leaves this consequential alternative visible here.

v20–25: A son's question is answered with the community's story: “we” were slaves, were brought out, and were brought in. The final verse retains the conditional language of righteousness and careful practice without adding a later doctrinal explanation.
v9: The written and read forms differ in the spelling of “his commands.” They represent one word, not two repeated commands. The read form is followed, and the whole source record is preserved.
v15: “Fiery snakes” retains the ancient description, commonly associated with the burning effect of a venomous bite. The wording does not say that the snakes literally breathe fire.
v1–5: Moses describes making a wooden ark and receiving new tablets. The translation retains his first-person account; compare the ark-making account in Exodus 37.

v6: The final expression can include the living things or possessions belonging to Dathan and Abiram, literally what was at their feet. The draft retains living things and their following or dependent relationship. Korah is not named in this verse.
